doc.title: Ralph LaLama interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 23, 2010

title: Students lacking talent: teaching them to teach and be fans
summary: He teaches such students to listen, teach, and become passionate fans.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Have you ever had a circumstance with a student who had the desire but really not the inherent talent?

Yes. Many times. Okay? And I teach him how to teach. I teach him how to listen. I teach him how to communicate with what they know, and they usually have the talent to absorb knowledge. And some of them have a talent to communicate. And as far as playing, yeah, but I still encourage them to play because it’s good therapy. You see if you’re a teacher you need therapy. But I can tell they’re never going to really get off the ground with it on a really high professional level, because they just don’t have the talent, but they really have the desire and they want to be involved. And you can be involved, as a teacher and even maybe a speaker, maybe a clinician. You don’t have to be a great player to be a clinician, you’ve just got to give out the right information.

And also a listener, a fan, teach them how to be a fan. I mean I know that sounds selfish but it’s not. You know this jazz world needs fans that are into it, that have a passion for it. The best fan is the guy that has a passion for it, not just somebody because they think it’s hip, you know, the flavor of the month. You know what I mean?
That’s an excellent answer to that question.
That’s the best answer I’ve got is to teach them to be a teacher or a jazz fan.
Or a fan, yeah. And they won’t have any problem with that because you know they can still get off. It’s a lot of satisfaction.
